messages.subject: lm() vs. rstanarm?
parts:
I know it's still early code, but ...

Here's a fit of cty to displ in the mpg data set from ggplot2:

,----
| > m1 <- lm(cty ~ displ, data = mpg)
| > display(m1)
| lm(formula = cty ~ displ, data = mpg)
| coef.est coef.se
| (Intercept) 25.99 0.48
| displ -2.63 0.13
| ---
| n = 234, k = 2
| residual sd = 2.57, R-Squared = 0.64
`----

and here's the same thing with rstanarm:

,----
| > s1 <- stanlm(cty ~ displ, data = mpg)
| > print(s1)
| Inference for Stan model: Gaussian GLM.
| 4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=1000; thin=1;
| post-warmup draws per chain=1000, total post-warmup draws=4000.
|
| mean se_mean sd 2.5% 25% 50% 75%
| (Intercept) 25.96 0.01 0.48 25.01 25.63 25.97 26.28
| displ -2.62 0.00 0.13 -2.87 -2.71 -2.62 -2.54
| sigma 2.58 0.00 0.12 2.36 2.50 2.58 2.66
| lp__ -337.64 0.04 1.27 -341.05 -338.19 -337.31 -336.73
| 97.5% n_eff Rhat
| (Intercept) 26.86 1281 1
| displ -2.37 1230 1
| sigma 2.84 1421 1
| lp__ -336.23 1012 1
|
| Samples were drawn using NUTS(diag_e) at Tue Dec 9 20:48:02 2014.
| For each parameter, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size,
| and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at
| convergence, Rhat=1).
`----

Am I missing something, or should the SE estimates be the same in both?

BTW, rstanarm looks like a really nice idea. Two thoughts:

- Some day an rstanarm::display function would be nice.
- It would be nice if stanlm and the other functions wrote the .stan
file in the cwd. That way, you could quickly generate the Stan code
and then modify it. In a different arena, Denemo and Lilypond work
that way in typesetting music.

Bill

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: lm() vs. rstanarm?
parts: Am I missing something, or should the SE estimates be the same in both?

Hi Bill,

The "sd" column from the output returned by stanlm() is the actual SD of the posterior distribution of the parameters.  The location of the posterior distribution can also vary if you ran the program again with a different seed, starting values, etc., which results in Monte Carlo error on top of the usual sampling error.  The "se_mean" column is an estimate of the Monte Carlo error, but the "sd" is the standard deviation of your posterior, which is analogous to the sampling-error estimate "SE" you see in output from lm() -- and those SEs for intercept and slope also match quite closely to the SDs of the posterior.  I forget what page it is on, but there should be more details in the Stan manual.

Terry

messages.author: b82af643aafe86d2
messages.subject: Re: lm() vs. rstanarm?
parts:
Terry,

Thanks (and d'oh).  Now I recall reading that somewhere, and it makes sense.  It was just a bit jarring to see (almost) the same term ("se*") used in two different ways on seemingly the same problem.

BTW, when I suggested an rstanarm::display() function would be nice some day, really the piece I missed was the formula.  While it makes sense for rstan::print() not to try to print the model, which could be pretty big, stanlm() and its relations should have formulas that are more like their non-Bayesian relatives.

Bill
